description: IgnitIQ turns 15+ years of NASA microgravity fire experiments into cited, data-backed fire safety guidance for future Moon and Mars habitats.
summary:
Ignit-IQ is an AI fire safety analyst built on 15+ years of real ISS combustion experiments. You pick a habitat atmosphere (ISS, Gateway, a lunar or Mars surface habitat, or Apollo 1 for reference), ask a fire safety question, and get an answer computed from actual test data and cited to the NASA investigation behind it.

Future habitats will run at lower pressure and higher oxygen than the ISS, and oxygen-rich air is what made the Apollo 1 and Mir fires so dangerous. Ignit-IQ shows how little of that space has been tested: 11 flight tests sit near the proposed lunar and Mars atmosphere, against 238 near ISS conditions.

Under the hood, Ignit-IQ joins 1,999 test rows from 18 flight investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics repository into one database. The AI agent runs SQL for every number and searches investigation text for explanations. Before any answer is shown, the system checks every number against a real query result. The LLM never estimates a figure. It scores 15 out of 15 on our evaluation set, runs on free open models, and costs $0 to operate.
details:
Live site: https://ignit-iq.vercel.app

Code: https://github.com/ana-lan/ignit-iq

API docs: https://ignit-iq.onrender.com/docs

(The free backend sleeps when idle. The first request can take about a minute to wake it.)

WHAT IT DOES

Ignit-IQ turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into answers a habitat designer can use. It has four views:

1. Mission brief: pick a habitat atmosphere and see ranked findings for it, plus a chart of every tested pressure and oxygen level with your habitat marked on it.

2. Experiment explorer: filter all 1,999 test rows by experiment, fuel, pressure and oxygen, with a link to each investigation's DOI.

3. Ask Ignit-IQ: a streaming chat. Every answer carries citations, and a "how I got this" drawer shows the SQL it ran, the passages it read and the check on every number.

4. Lessons: Apollo 1, Apollo 13 and Mir 1997, each linked to the findings that apply.

KEY FINDINGS FROM THE DATA

- Coverage gap: 11 tests sit near the proposed lunar and Mars habitat atmosphere (8.2 psia, 34% O2), against 238 near ISS conditions. That is 21.6x fewer.

- At 30% oxygen or more, 34% of CFI-G flames were still burning when the fuel flow was stopped. Below 25%, none were.

- CO2 put out FLEX droplet flames more often than nitrogen or helium (90% extinction vs 66% and 75%).

- In SAFFIRE-I, a flame spreading with the airflow burned about 6x longer than one spreading against it.

HOW IT WORKS

- Data: metadata, experimental tables and publication lists for 23 combustion investigations (18 flight, 5 ground) from NASA PSI. Every table was profiled by hand and mapped into one long "tests" table with a shared core schema (fuel, pressure in kPa, O2 fraction, diluent, flow, outcome, burn time). Each row keeps a link back to its source file and row.

- Two kinds of retrieval: numbers come from read-only SQL over DuckDB, and explanations come from vector search over investigation text, 350 publications and NASA incident pages.

- Agent: a hand-written tool loop with 4 tools (search_docs, query_tests, get_investigation, nearest_conditions). The SQL tool is locked to a single read-only SELECT with no external access, a row cap and a timeout.

- Verification: every number in an answer has to trace back to a tool result and match the citation on its sentence. If the check fails, the model gets one repair round that names the exact numbers that failed.

- Habitat presets come from NASA technical reports (NTRS) on exploration atmospheres.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Designers of lunar, Gateway and Mars habitats can see what flames actually did near their target atmosphere, and where no data exists yet. The coverage gap doubles as a test plan: it shows which pressure and oxygen conditions future ISS combustion experiments should cover next.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Most AI chat tools over documents guess at numbers. Ignit-IQ treats the experimental tables as the source of truth, shows its work, and says plainly when the data does not cover the conditions you asked about.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python 3.11, uv, httpx, pandas, pydantic, DuckDB, fastembed (BAAI bge-small-en-v1.5), NumPy, FastAPI, Server-Sent Events, Docker, Render. TypeScript, Next.js 15, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Recharts, SWR, Vercel. LLMs through OpenAI-compatible APIs: gpt-oss-120b and Qwen on Groq, Nemotron and Gemma on OpenRouter, with automatic fallback down the chain.

EVALUATION

15 questions with answer keys computed from the database, scored on the live API for correct numbers, citations, facts and grounding: 15/15. Median answer time 1.6 s.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Cost ($0, free open models), honesty (no estimated numbers, data gaps stated), citing every investigation by DOI as PSI requests, cold starts on free hosting (a "waking the backend" state plus cached demo answers), and known limits: some PSI tables are test logs with no measurements, and the verifier checks numbers, not meaning.

USE OF AI

AI coding assistants (Claude) helped write and debug the code and documentation. All code was run, checked and committed by me. At runtime, open LLMs write the chat answers. Every number they state is verified against SQL results before display. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used.

ADDITIONAL NASA SOURCES

Ground studies PSI-60 (Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets, https://doi.org/10.60555/mzjm-yv57) and PSI-62 (Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling vs BASS, https://doi.org/10.60555/e9xp-ex83). NASA history pages on the Apollo 1 fire, the Apollo 13 oxygen tank failure and the 1997 Mir fire, and NASA's 2015 Researcher's Guide to ISS Combustion Science. Links are in the repo's ingest/context.py, and every investigation DOI is in the README.
